newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia government split on fighting Khmer Rouge.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia government split on fighting Khmer Rouge.

text.p: Cambodia's government appeared sharply split on whether to back war against the rapidly unravelling Khmer Rouge whose reviled supremo Pol Pot remains on the run, officials and analysts said on Saturday.

Officials loyal to co-Premiers Prince Norodom Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who share power in an unhappy political alliance, presented clashing plans on how to best cope with the rebels responsible for the 1975-1979 "killing fields" regime.

Analysts said Ranariddh's side wants to arm breakaway rebels to hasten the movement's demise and forge political ties while Hun Sen was wary of tricks and wants to let the rebels left to fight it out among themselves.

Deputy chief of general staff Nhiek Bun Chhay on Saturday told reporters Pol Pot was holed up in the jungle east of his northern stronghold and about 1,000 breakaway rebels were closing in on his position.
The claim remained unconfirmed.
Nhiek Bun Chhay, who is loyal to Ranariddh and led talks with the Khmer Rouge on the prince's behalf, said troops from a government division had been sent to investigate.
He said he had also requested the Ministry of Defence to send weapons and ammunition to the 1,000 rebels thought to be fighting Pol Pot and about 250 to 300 of his followers.

Nhiek Bun Chhay said Pol Pot had taken top rebels, including Khieu Samphan, president of the guerrillas' provisional government, hostage. Ranariddh and Khieu Samphan have said they want to form a political alliance.
Hun Sen told reporters he doubted Pol Pot's top leaders, including right-hand man Nuon Chea, Khieu Samphan and northwest commander Ta Mok, were being held against their will.
Analysts agreed, noting Ranariddh had a lot to gain if the most notorious rebels disappeared and Khieu Samphan could later emerge as a more palatable political ally.
Hun Sen said no support should be given to any faction.
"I myself and...(my senior staff) have no plans to give any weapons, ammunitions or troops to Anlong Veng to help anyone because we are not sure," he said.

"We are sitting on a high mountain looking down on the two tigers until they become seriously wounded and then they will be easily captured," Hun Sen said, apparently referring to the two factions of the Khmer Rouge.

Analysts said the division in government policy was not a surprise. Ranariddh and Hun Sen, who formed an uneasy coalition after U.N.-sponsored polls in 1993, have been at odds over power-sharing issues and in fierce competition to recruit rebels to their own sides.

The Khmer Rouge, which have been fighting the government after reneging on a 1991 peace pact, have been decimated by thousands of defections since last August, when Pol Pot's brother-in-law, Ieng Sary broke from the Maoist guerrilla movement.
The rebels now appear on their last legs, but their ability to divide Cambodia's leaders has not diminished, analysts said.
"As with everything, both sides of the government are at odds and seeing what mileage they can get out of this," said one political analyst.
Ranariddh is in a hurry to form a political alliance with Khieu Samphan, while Hun Sen has reacted by calling any talks with the rebel "an illegal negotiation," the analyst said.
Reflecting that disagreement, an adviser to Hun Sen told Reuters Nhiek Bun Chhay's plan to arm rebels was unacceptable.
"They are terrorists. Let them fight among themselves. The government should leave them to themselves and then take final action when they stop fighting," he said.
